HiNa-MoE: High-Performance, Non-Intrusive MoE Inference on CPUs with Matrix Engines

Conference: International Conference on Parallel Architectures and Compilation Techniques; October 19-22, 2026; Chicago, IL, USAInternational Conference on Parallel Architectures and Compilation Techniques (PACT ’26), October 19-22, 2026, Chicago, IL, USADOI: 10.1145/3838684.3846846ISBN: 979-8-4007-2915-7/2026/10
Weiling Yang Note: Equal Contribution Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China email: w.yang@nudt.edu.cn , Junwen Zhang Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China email: zhang_junwen@nudt.edu.cn , Dezun Dong Note: Corresponding author Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China email: dong@nudt.edu.cn , Jianbin Fang Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China email: j.fang@nudt.edu.cn , Enda Yu Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China email: yuenda@nudt.edu.cn , Zhe Bai Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China email: baizheo3o@nudt.edu.cn and Xiaopeng Deng Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China email: dengxiaopeng25@nudt.edu.cn

Abstract.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference is increasingly deployed in local and on-premise environments, where expert parameters often exceed GPU memory capacity. In latency-sensitive, low-concurrency settings, repeatedly staging routed-expert weights from CPU memory to the GPU can be prohibitive, leaving routed-expert feed-forward networks (FFNs) on the critical path of multi-socket CPUs. Existing CPU accelerations often rely on intrusive, hardware- or topology-specific requirements, such as AMX-specific weight layouts or manual NUMA-aware placement. These requirements reduce portability and complicate integration with standard CPU–GPU offloading pipelines. We present HiNa-MoE, a high-performance, non-intrusive operator library for MoE inference on CPUs with matrix engines. HiNa-MoE (1) exploits AMX with an optimized micro-kernel that keeps expert weights in standard layouts and instead fuses lightweight layout transforms into token gathering and stores; (2) applies NUMA-aware task partitioning that minimizes cross-socket traffic under a simple page-interleaved policy without modifying the framework allocator; and (3) converts decode-phase memory-bound matrix–vector operations into small matrix–matrix execution to better utilize AMX. Across multiple server-class CPUs and real-world MoE models, HiNa-MoE achieves up to 3.37×\times speedup for FFN kernels and up to 2.09×\times end-to-end inference speedup over state-of-the-art baselines, while remaining plug-and-play with existing frameworks and deployment workflows.

Keywords: 
Mixture-of-Experts, CPU Inference, NUMA Optimization, AMX, Non-Intrusive Design

1. Introduction

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models (LLMs) offer an appealing quality–efficiency trade-off by using conditional computation: each token activates only a small subset of experts in the feed-forward network (FFN) layers (Fedus et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024; Yang et al., 2025). This sparsity reduces arithmetic work relative to dense LLMs while preserving high model capacity, and it has become a common design point in production models such as Mixtral (, 2025), Qwen-MoE (, 2025), and DeepSeek (, 2025).

Problem scope. In local and on-premise deployments, MoE inference increasingly runs on CPU–GPU nodes with limited GPU memory (, 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2025; Kamahori et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; , 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). Since the complete set of expert parameters can exceed GPU memory capacity, practical systems often keep some or all routed experts in CPU DRAM and execute different experts on the CPU and GPU (Chen et al., 2025; Kamahori et al., 2025; , 2025; Yu et al., 2026). Thus, MoE inference in this setting is inherently a heterogeneous CPU–GPU execution problem: depending on the inference workload, a routed expert may be executed either on the CPU or on the GPU.

A natural strategy is to execute routed experts on the GPU whenever they are activated. However, the benefit of GPU execution depends strongly on the number of tokens processed by each expert. At large batch sizes, the cost of transferring expert weights can be amortized over more tokens, making GPU execution attractive (Cao et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025). In contrast, during low-concurrency inference, each expert typically processes only a small number of tokens, while its weights remain large. Repeatedly transferring expert weights from CPU memory to the GPU can therefore incur substantial data-movement overhead relative to the computation (Yu et al., 2026; Kamahori et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). In such cases, retaining routed experts in CPU memory and executing their FFNs on the CPU can be preferable. Figure 1 illustrates this trade-off: CPU execution remains competitive at small and moderate batch sizes, whereas GPU execution becomes increasingly advantageous as the batch size grows.

This workload-dependent execution behavior defines the scope of our work. We do not attempt to redesign the CPU–GPU offloading or scheduling policy. Instead, we focus on the CPU execution path, which remains critical when routed experts are retained in CPU memory under low-concurrency workloads. Our goal is to make CPU-side expert execution highly efficient and portable, while preserving the standard weight layouts required by existing GPU libraries. In this way, HiNa-MoE serves as a CPU-side building block for heterogeneous MoE inference: existing or future offloading policies can continue to choose between CPU and GPU execution, while HiNa-MoE provides an efficient CPU backend when CPU execution is selected.

Challenge. CPU-based MoE inference is constrained by (1) small/irregular matrix multiplications (few tokens per expert) and (2) cross-socket memory traffic when expert weights reside in CPU DRAM. To exploit matrix engines such as Intel AMX, systems including KTransformers (Chen et al., 2025) and Intel Extension for PyTorch (IPEX) (, 2025) store expert weights in AMX-specific layouts. While effective for CPU execution, such layouts are incompatible with standard GPU libraries, complicating CPU–GPU offloading and forcing reconversion, duplicated storage, or specialized kernels. Meanwhile, to mitigate cross-NUMA traffic, KTransformers further partitions weight tensors across NUMA nodes, requiring deep modifications to the inference framework and its memory allocation behavior. Together, these choices improve speed but reduce portability and raise the engineering barrier for real deployments.

Our approach. We present HiNa-MoE, a CPU-optimized library for MoE operators that delivers high performance while remaining non-intrusive: it requires no offline weight reformatting, no framework-level weight sharding, and no custom NUMA-aware allocator (Section 3.1). HiNa-MoE preserves general-purpose matrix layouts (row- or column-major) and requires no changes to the framework’s weight storage or memory allocation policies; adopting it amounts to replacing a small, well-defined set of operator implementations.

Contributions. HiNa-MoE achieves these goals via three complementary techniques:

  • •

    AMX-efficient micro-kernels for general layouts. Based on observations of MoE FFN computation patterns and AMX data layout constraints, we design micro-kernels that keep expert weights in standard layouts and instead fuse lightweight layout transforms into token gathering and stores (“transform intermediate matrix, not weight matrix”), enabling efficient AMX utilization without any weight reformatting (Section 4).

  • •

    NUMA-aware task partitioning without framework modifications. Leveraging the fact that expert dimensions in modern MoE models are typically multiples of 128 (, 2025; , 2025; , 2025), we propose a task-partitioning strategy that reduces cross-socket traffic under a simple page-interleaved policy (e.g., numactl --interleave=all) without restructuring weight storage (Section 5).

  • •

    Attention optimization via MV-to-MM conversion. During decoding, we convert memory-intensive matrix–vector operations into compute-intensive matrix–matrix execution to better utilize AMX (Section 6).

Results. We evaluate HiNa-MoE on three representative multi-core CPUs: Intel Xeon Gold 6430 (, 2025), 6448H (, 2025), and Max 9462 (, 2025). Across real-world MoE models (, 2025; , 2025; , 2025), HiNa-MoE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines (Chen et al., 2025; , 2025; , 2025), achieving up to 3.37×\times FFN-kernel speedup and up to 2.09×\times end-to-end inference speedup. These results make HiNa-MoE a practical and portable building block for high-performance MoE inference on CPU–GPU nodes.

2. Background and Related Work

2.1. MoE Architecture

MoE models are built by stacking Transformer layers (Cao et al., 2025), where each layer consists of an attention module followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). In standard dense models (e.g., OPT (Zhang et al., 2022) and LLaMA-3 (Team, 2024)), every token is processed by the same FFN. In contrast, an MoE layer replaces this single FFN with multiple independent expert FFNs and uses a gating function to route each token to only a small subset of experts. As shown in Figure 2, tokens are first processed by attention and then dispatched to the selected experts, which introduces structured sparsity in both computation and memory traffic.

2.2. Advanced CPU Compute Unit

Modern CPUs integrate matrix engines such as Intel AMX (, 2025) and Arm SME (, 2025), which provide substantially higher throughput than SIMD units (e.g., AVX-512) for matrix workloads. However, these gains often rely on specific data layouts and incur packing/transform overheads (Chen et al., 2025). In this work, we focus on AMX, which is widely available in current server CPUs (where SME is not yet broadly deployed).

Figure 3 illustrates the BF16 fused multiply–add (FMA) workflow of AMX. For simplicity, matrices are shown as 4×164\times 16 bytes. Each core provides eight tile registers (tmm0∼\simtmm7), each of size 16×\times64 bytes. In the figure, matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} matches the layout expected by tmm0 (row-major, reduction along columns), which is also a common layout in both CPU and GPU libraries. In contrast, matrix 𝐁\mathbf{B} does not match the layout required by tmm1; consequently, 𝐁\mathbf{B} is typically transformed into an AMX-specific layout prior to computation. We refer to the layout expected by tmm0 as the general layout and the layout expected by tmm1 as the AMX-specific layout.

2.3. NUMA Architecture

Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) is the dominant architecture for multi-socket servers. In a NUMA system, a core can access memory attached to its local node with higher bandwidth and lower latency than memory attached to a remote node (cross-NUMA access) (, 2025). NUMA systems typically expose three memory allocation policies:

  • •

    First-touch: the default OS policy; a page is allocated on the node of the thread that first writes it. This is convenient but can lead to non-deterministic and suboptimal placement.

  • •

    Interleaved: pages are allocated round-robin across all nodes. This policy is deterministic and easy to deploy (e.g., via numactl --interleave=all) without code modifications.

  • •

    NUMA-aware: the application explicitly allocates pages on specific nodes to optimize locality, but this typically requires invasive code changes.

HiNa-MoE shows that, when combined with NUMA-aware task partitioning, the simple interleaved policy can mitigate cross-NUMA bottlenecks without modifying the inference framework’s weight storage or memory allocator.

2.4. Related Work

In resource-constrained scenarios, MoE inference systems typically combine (i) a high-level policy for placing experts and scheduling transfers across CPU and GPU and (ii) a low-level implementation of operators (FFN and attention). We therefore organize related work along three axes: offloading/scheduling, CPU operator kernels and data layouts, and NUMA locality management (Chen et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Kamahori et al., 2025; , 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Du et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025).

2.4.1. Offloading and scheduling

LIA (Kim et al., 2025) adapts offloading decisions based on prompt length, batch size, and inference phase for dense LLMs. MoE-Lightning (Cao et al., 2025) pages expert weights to GPU memory and overlaps transfers with GPU FFN execution. Fiddler (Kamahori et al., 2025) proposes a dynamic offloading strategy and finds that substantial GPU offloading gains occur only beyond a batch-size threshold. HybriMoE designs prefetching to proactively fetch frequently invoked (“hot”) experts to increase GPU residency (Zhong et al., 2025). KTransformers (Chen et al., 2025) uses a static placement strategy, retaining routed experts on the CPU while placing shared experts and attention layers on the GPU.

Key differentiation. HiNa-MoE does not propose a new offloading policy. Instead, we focus on making CPU-side operators both fast and portable so they can serve as drop-in building blocks under existing and future policies.

2.4.2. CPU operator optimization and data layouts

KTransformers (Chen et al., 2025) and IPEX (, 2025) accelerate CPU-side MoE operators by leveraging AMX, typically through pre-converting expert weights into AMX-specific layouts (e.g., tmm1 in Figure 3). T-MAC (Wei et al., 2025) targets low-bit dense LLM inference on embedded CPUs by transforming matrix multiply–accumulate operations into table lookups.

Why “layout-first” can be intrusive. AMX-specific layouts can improve CPU throughput, but they hinder heterogeneous execution because standard GPU libraries expect general layouts. In practice, this often forces extra weight conversions (AMX-specific layout→\rightarrow general layout) or the use of specialized GPU kernels. Retaining general layouts is therefore essential for seamless CPU–GPU collaborative execution of routed expert FFNs.

2.4.3. NUMA locality management

On multi-socket servers, cross-NUMA bandwidth and latency can dominate MoE decoding. KTransformers reduces remote traffic by partitioning each weight tensor across NUMA nodes and using tensor-parallel execution so each socket primarily accesses local expert weights (Chen et al., 2025).

Key differentiation. KTransformers and IPEX are the closest baselines to HiNa-MoE for CPU-side MoE execution with AMX. HiNa-MoE differs in two key ways. First, instead of requiring AMX-specific weight layouts, we preserve general layouts and apply on-the-fly transformations to the intermediate matrix during kernel execution, maintaining compatibility with standard GPU libraries and CPU–GPU offloading frameworks. Second, on multi-socket servers, we avoid framework-level custom NUMA-aware allocators by combining OS-level page interleaving with NUMA-aware task partitioning to reduce cross-socket traffic (Table 1).

3. Motivation

3.1. The Case for a Non-Intrusive Design

In local deployments, MoE inference often runs on multi-socket CPU–GPU nodes, where expert parameters reside in CPU DRAM and CPU-side execution becomes performance-critical. Meanwhile, the operator stack must remain easy to integrate across CPU-only, GPU-offload, and hybrid settings (, 2025; Kim et al., 2025). We argue that this requires a non-intrusive design with two principles:

  • •

    General layouts: expert weights remain in standard row- or column-major formats compatible with CPU and GPU libraries.

  • •

    Framework agnosticism: no changes to weight storage, tensor semantics, or memory allocation.

These principles preserve deployment flexibility: models can move between CPU and GPU without layout conversion or duplication, and NUMA effects can be handled via OS-level mechanisms (e.g., numactl --interleave=all) rather than intrusive changes.

Non-intrusive criterion. A method is non-intrusive if it requires no (1) offline weight reformatting, (2) framework-level weight sharding/replication changes, or (3) custom NUMA-aware allocators. HiNa-MoE satisfies these by preserving general layouts, using page interleaving, and applying NUMA-aware task partitioning (Table 1).

Table 1 shows that existing systems trade off performance, portability, and complexity: some retain generality but underutilize CPU performance (e.g., Fiddler), while others achieve high performance via intrusive, hardware-specific optimizations (e.g., IPEX, KTransformers). HiNa-MoE breaks this trade-off without sacrificing deployability.

3.2. Limitations of Previous Works

To quantify the cost of this trade-off, we evaluate representative systems along two hardware-critical dimensions: (i) AMX utilization and (ii) NUMA locality on multi-socket nodes.

AMX layout overhead. To satisfy AMX’s layout requirements, frameworks typically adopt one of two strategies. Runtime conversion (e.g., oneDNN) stores weights in a general layout and transforms them on the fly during expert execution; this preserves compatibility, but introduces a recurring conversion overhead. Pre-conversion (e.g., IPEX and KTransformers) stores weights in an AMX-specific layout, maximizing AMX throughput but making the weights incompatible with standard GPU libraries; CPU–GPU offloading then requires a costly reverse transformation, duplicated weight storage, or bespoke GPU kernels.

Cross-socket (NUMA) penalty. Figure 4 shows that memory-bandwidth utilization drops by about 20% when scaling from one to two NUMA nodes. Systems without NUMA-aware execution (e.g., IPEX and oneDNN) incur substantial cross-socket traffic, reducing effective bandwidth available to memory-bound MoE operators. KTransformers mitigates this by pre-partitioning weights across NUMA nodes to enforce locality, but doing so is intrusive and requires modifying tensor storage as well as the framework’s memory allocation behavior.

Overall, current approaches either leave performance untapped or bake in hardware-specific assumptions that reduce portability and increase engineering cost. This motivates an operator stack that delivers high performance without intrusion.

Motivated by this gap, HiNa-MoE is designed to pursue three goals simultaneously: (1) preserve general matrix layouts to maximize offloading flexibility, (2) fully exploit AMX compute capability, and (3) avoid cross-NUMA accesses without framework modifications.

4. Exploiting AMX With General Layouts

4.1. Overview and Design Philosophy

Figure 5 illustrates the computation pattern of an expert FFN, where each expert is activated by only a subset of tokens. To improve efficiency, inference frameworks first gather the activated tokens into an intermediate matrix 𝐈\mathbf{I}, so that the expert computation becomes a small number of matrix–matrix multiplications (MM) instead of many matrix–vector multiplications. Token gathering is a standard step in modern MoE runtimes and is essential for efficient FFN execution on both CPU and GPU (, 2025; Chen et al., 2025; , 2026).

Given 𝐈\mathbf{I}, the expert FFN computes two projections (with 𝐖𝐠𝐚𝐭𝐞\mathbf{W_{gate}} and 𝐖𝐮𝐩\mathbf{W_{up}}), applies a nonlinearity (e.g., SiLU), combines the two branches via element-wise multiplication, and then applies 𝐖𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧\mathbf{W_{down}}. We write the expert FFN as

FFN⁡(𝐈)=SiLU⁡(𝐈×𝐖𝐠𝐚𝐭𝐞)⊙(𝐈×𝐖𝐮𝐩)×𝐖𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧\small\mathrm{FFN}(\mathbf{I})=\mathrm{SiLU}(\mathbf{I}\times\mathbf{W_{gate}})\odot(\mathbf{I}\times\mathbf{W_{up}})\times\mathbf{W_{down}}

where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication.

Why general layouts matter. In mainstream MoE inference frameworks (, 2025), token matrices, expert weights, and output tensors are stored in a unified, general-purpose layout (typically row-major) so the same model state can support both CPU and GPU execution (Figure 6). However, AMX reaches peak throughput only when one MM operand is in an AMX-specific (packed) layout (Section 2.2). To avoid per-inference layout conversion, IPEX and KTransformers pre-convert each expert weight matrix 𝐖\mathbf{W} into an AMX-specific layout (Figure ). While this improves CPU performance, the resulting weight format is incompatible with standard GPU libraries, which makes CPU–GPU offloading inflexible and can force reconversion or special-purpose kernels.

Our approach: transform 𝐈\mathbf{I}, not 𝐖\mathbf{W}. HiNa-MoE achieves high AMX performance while preserving the framework’s general layouts (Figure ). This design remains largely unexplored (, 2025; Chen et al., 2025) due to the unclear interaction between AMX and MoE FFN computation. Instead of pre-converting weights, we perform lightweight runtime layout transformations on the intermediate matrix 𝐈\mathbf{I} and fuse them into data movement that the framework already must perform. Concretely, during token gathering, the selected tokens are loaded into registers and written into 𝐈\mathbf{I}. We fuse a register-level transformation into this path so that 𝐈\mathbf{I} is produced directly in an AMX-specific layout (the first transformation in Figure ). The overhead is small because (i) 𝐈\mathbf{I} is much smaller than the expert weight matrices and (ii) the transform consists of only a handful of register operations.

Specifically, matrix 𝐈\mathbf{I} corresponds to the tile register labeled tmm1 in Figure 3; this mapping preserves the mathematical form 𝐈×𝐖\mathbf{I}\times\mathbf{W}. After computing 𝐈×𝐖𝐠𝐚𝐭𝐞\mathbf{I}\times\mathbf{W_{gate}} and 𝐈×𝐖𝐮𝐩\mathbf{I}\times\mathbf{W_{up}}, we similarly fuse the store path to emit outputs in the layout required by the next AMX MM (the second transformation). Finally, after multiplying by 𝐖𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧\mathbf{W_{down}}, we apply a register-level transpose before writing the output back in the standard row-major layout (the third transformation).

In summary, we keep expert weights in the general layout (tmm0 in Figure 3) and align 𝐈\mathbf{I} with the AMX-specific operand (tmm1), fusing necessary transforms into unavoidable gather/store operations. This redesign is confined to the FFN operator implementation and requires no changes to the framework’s matrix layouts. HiNa-MoE therefore enables the framework to fully exploit AMX without requiring the framework to be aware of AMX-specific layout constraints.

4.2. Micro-kernel Design

4.2.1. Determining Micro-kernel Size

Expert FFN performance is dominated by its three MM operators, so micro-kernel efficiency is a first-order concern. We target high efficiency by maximizing the compute-to-memory ratio (CMR) of the micro-kernel (Yang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2015; Heinecke et al., 2016), which captures how much arithmetic we can perform per byte loaded from memory.

Many prior designs are primarily tuned for vector registers and fall back to vector units (e.g., AVX-512) when the row dimension of 𝐈\mathbf{I} is small; for example, KTransformers uses AMX only when the row dimension exceeds four (Chen et al., 2025). In contrast, HiNa-MoE uses AMX for all row dimensions and focuses on maximizing reuse within AMX tile registers even in the decoding regime.

We describe the micro-kernel in BF16, but the same sizing methodology applies to other precisions. Let the micro-kernel tile sizes be mrm_{r} (rows), nrn_{r} (columns), and krk_{r} (reduction). AMX tiles support up to 64 bytes along the reduction dimension, corresponding to 32 BF16 elements. Because MoE weight dimensions are typically multiples of 32 (, 2025; , 2025; , 2025), we set kr=32k_{r}=32 to maximize tile utilization (e.g., DeepSeek-V3 uses 7,168 and 2,048; Mixtral-8x7B uses 4,096 and 14,336).

In one micro-kernel step, AMX tiles hold mr⋅32m_{r}\cdot 32 elements of 𝐈\mathbf{I}, nr⋅32n_{r}\cdot 32 elements of 𝐖\mathbf{W}, and mr⋅nrm_{r}\cdot n_{r} FP32 accumulators. Each core provides eight 1,024-byte tile registers, which constrains mrm_{r} and nrn_{r} as follows:

(1) {mr⋅64+nr⋅64+mr⋅nr⋅4⩽8⋅1024mr⩽M\small\left\{\begin{matrix}m_{r}\cdot 64+n_{r}\cdot 64+m_{r}\cdot n_{r}\cdot 4\leqslant 8\cdot 1024\\ m_{r}\leqslant M\end{matrix}\right.

where MM is the row dimension of 𝐈\mathbf{I}. Each AMX FMA consumes BF16 inputs and accumulates into FP32 (4 bytes), which explains the ⋅4\cdot 4 term.

Each step performs 2⋅mr⋅nr⋅322\cdot m_{r}\cdot n_{r}\cdot 32 operations (a multiplication and an addition) and loads only 𝐈\mathbf{I} and 𝐖\mathbf{W} because the accumulators remain resident in tile registers. Thus,

(2) C​M​R=2⋅mr⋅nr⋅32mr⋅64+nr⋅64=mr⋅nrmr+nr\small CMR=\frac{2\cdot m_{r}\cdot n_{r}\cdot 32}{m_{r}\cdot 64+n_{r}\cdot 64}=\frac{m_{r}\cdot n_{r}}{m_{r}+n_{r}}

Combining Equations 1 and 2, the CMR is maximized at mr=nr=32m_{r}=n_{r}=32. When M<32M<32, we set mr=Mm_{r}=M to match the available rows.

4.2.2. Implementation Details

Algorithm 1 outlines the implementation of our AMX MM micro-kernel. When M≤32M\leq 32, expert weights exhibit limited temporal reuse in the cache; we therefore load 𝐖\mathbf{W} using the tileloadt1 instruction. tileloadt1 performs non-temporal loads that reduce cache pollution and do not trigger hardware prefetching, improving the effective use of main-memory bandwidth under decoding-style access patterns.

The second and third layout transformations in Figure  are fused into the micro-kernel (line 5 of Algorithm 1). These transformations execute within registers and the L1 data cache, and therefore introduce negligible overhead, which we also validate experimentally.

5. Non-Intrusive Cross-NUMA Optimization

5.1. Performance Bottleneck and Opportunity

In CPU-centric MoE inference on multi-socket servers, the dominant NUMA bottleneck is remote access to expert weight matrices (Chen et al., 2025). In contrast, accesses to the gathered token matrix 𝐈\mathbf{I} are typically not performance-critical. During prefill, MM is determined by batch size, prompt length, and expert activation rate, and in common local deployments the batch size is small (often 1). When prompts are short, 𝐈\mathbf{I} is much smaller than the expert weights; when prompts are long, prefill becomes compute-bound and is commonly addressed via CPU-GPU or multi-GPU parallelism, which is outside our scope. During decoding, MM equals the batch size times the activation rate, and 𝐈\mathbf{I} remains small.

To avoid cross-socket traffic on weights, prior systems such as KTransformers use numa_alloc_onnode to partition each weight matrix across NUMA nodes so that each socket primarily accesses its local portion (Figure 7(a)). However, this approach is intrusive because it requires modifying the framework’s tensor storage and memory allocator.

HiNa-MoE instead relies on a standard OS mechanism: interleaving the physical pages of weight matrices across NUMA nodes (e.g., via numactl --interleave=all). With 4 KB pages, each page holds 2,048 BF16 elements; for example, a weight matrix with 6,144 columns occupies three pages per row (Figure 7(b)). Given this page-level interleaving, HiNa-MoE uses task partitioning so that each socket predominantly touches pages local to its NUMA node, while preserving the framework’s original weight storage.

5.2. Task Partitioning Strategy

Under an interleaved page layout, high MM performance requires two properties: (1) each socket should primarily read weight elements that are local to its NUMA node, and (2) each socket must still be able to assemble contiguous tiles that efficiently feed AMX (in particular, the operand mapped to tmm0 in Figure 3).

With explicit NUMA placement (e.g., numa_alloc_onnode), these properties are straightforward to satisfy: adjacent matrix rows stored on the same node can be mapped directly to AMX tile rows (Figure 8(a)). Under page interleaving, however, adjacent rows can reside on different NUMA nodes. For example, in Figure 7(b), the first 2,048 elements of row 0 are on NUMA 0, while the first 2,048 elements of row 1 are on NUMA 1.

As a result, as shown in Figure 8(b), on NUMA 0 we may need to combine segments from non-adjacent rows to fill AMX tile rows (e.g., elements 0∼20470\sim 2047 of row 0 and elements 0∼20470\sim 2047 of row 2), while selecting multiple segments within a row to cover the reduction dimension (e.g., elements 0∼20470\sim 2047 and 4096∼61434096\sim 6143 of row 0). Next, we show how to systematically identify and organize these segments.

Concretely, we address three subproblems: (1) identifying which weight segments are local to each NUMA node under interleaving; (2) selecting local segments that share the same yy-range so they can form AMX tile rows; and (3) selecting local segments that share the same xx so they provide contiguous ranges along the reduction dimension. Subproblem (1) enforces locality, while (2) and (3) ensure efficient utilization of AMX.

For ease of description, we define the following terms.

xx and yy: the coordinates of an element in the weight matrix along the row and reduction dimensions, respectively. For example, the labels 0, 2047, and 4096 in Figure 7 indicate yy-coordinates.

Data segment (x,ys​t​a​r​t∼ye​n​d)(x,\ y_{start}\sim y_{end}): a contiguous range of elements in the same row, from ys​t​a​r​ty_{start} to ye​n​dy_{end} along the reduction dimension. For example, the first segment in Figure 7(b) is (0,0∼2047)(0,0\sim 2047).

Function f⁡(x,y)f(x,y): the page-level “vertical” coordinate used to determine the NUMA placement under interleaving. We define

(3) f⁡(x,y)=(x⋅K+y)mod(2048⋅Nn​u​m​a),x∈[0,N),y∈[0,K)\small f(x,y)=(x\cdot K+y)\bmod(2048\cdot N_{numa}),\ x\in[0,N),\ y\in[0,K)

Here, NN and KK are the row and reduction dimensions of the weight matrix, and Nn​u​m​aN_{numa} is the number of NUMA nodes. The function f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) is periodic with period

(4) Tx=2048⋅Nn​u​m​agcd⁡(K,2048⋅Nn​u​m​a)∈[0,N),Ty=2048⋅Nn​u​m​a∈[0,K)\small\begin{split}T_{x}&=\frac{2048\cdot N_{numa}}{\gcd(K,2048\cdot N_{numa})}\in[0,N),\\ T_{y}&=2048\cdot N_{numa}\in[0,K)\end{split}

where TxT_{x}, TyT_{y} are the periods in xx and yy. Based on the characteristics of the periodic function, namely f⁡(x,y)=f⁡(x+Tx,y+Ty)f(x,y)=f(x+T_{x},y+T_{y}), it can be concluded that the data segment (x,ys​t​a​r​t∼ye​n​d)(x,y_{start}\sim y_{end}) and the data segment (x+Tx,ys​t​a​r​t+Ty∼ye​n​d+Ty)(x+T_{x},y_{start}+T_{y}\sim y_{end}+T_{y}) are guaranteed to reside on the same NUMA node. Therefore, we only need to identify the data segments within the first period of xx; the remaining data segments can be derived based on the properties of the periodic function. All data on each NUMA node must satisfy the following constraints:

(5) i​dn​u​m​a⋅2048<=f⁡(x,y)<(i​dn​u​m​a+1)⋅2048i​dn​u​m​a∈[0,Nn​u​m​a),x∈[0,Tx)\small\begin{split}id_{numa}\cdot 2048<=f(x,y)<(id_{numa}+1)\cdot 2048\\ \hskip 9.24994ptid_{numa}\in[0,N_{numa}),x\in[0,T_{x})\end{split}

i​dn​u​m​aid_{numa} denotes the id of a NUMA node.

TxT_{x} is usually very small, and this follows from two observations. First, in modern MoE models, the dimensions of expert weight matrices (i.e., hidden_size and intermediate_size) are typically multiples of 128. This is not accidental: widely used model families such as Qwen (, 2025), DeepSeek (, 2025), and Mixtral (, 2025) all exhibit this property. Second, mainstream server platforms most commonly expose two NUMA nodes, while four-node systems are comparatively rare. For example, in Mixtral-8x7B, KK takes values 4,096 or 14,336; on a dual-socket system, Equation 4 yields Tx=1T_{x}=1 and Tx=2T_{x}=2, respectively. Similarly, in Qwen3-30B-A3B, K=2,048K=2,048 or 768, corresponding to Tx=2T_{x}=2 and Tx=16T_{x}=16. Because the period TxT_{x} is small, we only need to traverse the first period of xx. For each fixed xx in this interval, we can identify the corresponding yy-ranges. The lower and upper bounds of each such yy-range are exactly the ys​t​a​r​ty_{start} and ye​n​dy_{end} values of a local data segment.

In summary, the data segments assigned to each NUMA node can be derived in two steps. First, compute TxT_{x} and TyT_{y} from the weight shape and the number of NUMA nodes using Equation 4. Second, determine the data segments for each NUMA node within the first period of xx using Equation 5, which solves subproblem (1). Segments with the same xx are then used to assemble contiguous ranges along the reduction dimension of the AMX tile registers, while segments sharing the same ys​t​a​r​ty_{start} and ye​n​dy_{end} are used to assemble the tile rows. This addresses subproblems (2) and (3). Taking the weight matrix in Figure 7(b) as an example, we have Tx=2T_{x}=2 and Ty=4096T_{y}=4096. For NUMA 0, when x=0x=0 we obtain y∈[0,2048)y\in[0,2048) and y∈[4096,6144)y\in[4096,6144), and when x=1x=1 we obtain y∈[2048,4096)y\in[2048,4096). Based on these three segments, all segments on NUMA 0 can be derived. In the implementation, we do not need to explicitly materialize the remaining segments; the kernel can index the weight tensor using only these segments together with TxT_{x}, which is sufficient to ensure correct and local computation.

Although our design leverages the facts that current MoE models use 128-aligned dimensions and that commercial servers expose only a small number of NUMA nodes, these are not arbitrary assumptions; rather, they arise naturally from both hardware constraints and common model design choices. Overall, HiNa-MoE enables the framework to minimize cross-NUMA accesses to expert weights without requiring the framework to be aware of NUMA details.

5.3. Design Details

To fit the task partitioning in Section 5.2, we make several adjustments to the micro-kernel, as shown in Algorithm 2. We use the array Si​n​d​e​xS_{index} to store the indices of the data segments assigned to each node, containing only the data segments within a single period of xx (i.e., x<Txx<T_{x}). Each entry of the array contains three elements: xx, ys​t​a​r​ty_{start}, and ye​n​dy_{end}.

Line 1 of Algorithm 2 iterates over one period of xx. For a fixed xx, all local data segments are processed along the reduction dimension, which is implemented by the loop in Line 3. Specifically, segments that share the same xx are multiplied with the corresponding elements of 𝐈\mathbf{I}, and the partial results are accumulated into tile registers tmm4∼\simtmm7 (Lines 2 and 7). To fully utilize the two tile registers used for the 𝐖\mathbf{W} operand, 32 segments of 𝐖\mathbf{W} that share the same yy coordinate are loaded from the local NUMA node in each iteration (Line 6), where the xx coordinate of adjacent segments differs by TxT_{x}. Since the reduction dimension of 𝐖\mathbf{W} may span multiple NUMA nodes (Figure 7(b)), each node computes a partial result using only its local segments. After all NUMA nodes finish, the partial results are aggregated to produce the final output.

6. Attention Module Optimization

The attention module consists of (i) input projections (three matrix multiplications, producing 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, 𝐊\mathbf{K}, and 𝐕\mathbf{V}), (ii) scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), and (iii) an output projection (one matrix multiplication). The projection MMs are optimized by our AMX micro-kernels (Section 4) together with the NUMA-aware task partitioning strategy (Section 5.2), and therefore we focus here on SDPA. Prior work has largely optimized SDPA for the prefill phase (Fu et al., 2024; Dao et al., 2022), where computation dominates and batching is higher. We therefore target SDPA optimization in decoding.

6.1. SDPA Module Optimization

Modern MoE models commonly use grouped-query attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023) to reduce KV-cache size while maintaining accuracy (e.g., Qwen and Mixtral). During decoding, the query 𝐐\mathbf{Q} is split into hqh_{q} heads, where each head is a length-dd vector. The key 𝐊\mathbf{K} and value 𝐕\mathbf{V} are split into hk​vh_{kv} heads, where each head is a matrix of size ls​e​q×dl_{seq}\times d (Figure 9). Here, dd denotes the head dimension and ls​e​ql_{seq} denotes the current sequence length.

In GQA, each key/value head is shared by a group of hqhk​v\frac{h_{q}}{h_{kv}} query heads. Consequently, computing attention scores for one KV head can be expressed as multiplying a small block of query heads (shape hqhk​v×d\frac{h_{q}}{h_{kv}}\times d) with the corresponding key head (shape ls​e​q×dl_{seq}\times d), i.e., a MM. The same structure appears again when multiplying attention probabilities by the value head, and thus the decode-phase SDPA kernel naturally exposes a sequence of small MMs.

To exploit AMX in these decode-phase MMs, HiNa-MoE performs lightweight, on-the-fly layout transformations on the small query-head block and keeps the transformed block resident in cache across the subsequent multiplies. Because hqhk​v\frac{h_{q}}{h_{kv}} is small (e.g., 8 in Qwen3-30B-A3B (, 2025)), the transformation cost is negligible relative to the MM work. For the subsequent multiplication with 𝐕\mathbf{V}, HiNa-MoE similarly converts the accessed value-head tiles into an AMX-specific layout on demand, enabling high AMX utilization without changing the framework’s native tensor layouts.

7. Experimental Setup

7.1. Hardware Details

We evaluate HiNa-MoE on two modern multi-socket server platforms: a dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6430 (6430) (, 2025) and a quad-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6448H (6448H) (, 2025) (Table 2). Memory bandwidth is measured using STREAM (, 2025). The local (per-socket) bandwidth and cross-socket bandwidth quantify the cost of NUMA-remote accesses. Although both CPUs support eight memory channels per socket, our 6448H machine is populated with only six memory modules per socket, resulting in lower measured local bandwidth than the fully populated 6430. The 6430 system also includes an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (, 2025) for hybrid CPU–GPU experiments (Chen et al., 2025), whereas the 6448H system is CPU-only.

7.2. Competitive Baselines

We compare HiNa-MoE against four widely used CPU(-centric) inference stacks. All baseline configurations follow the official recommendations.

IPEX (, 2025): Intel Extension for PyTorch, which optimizes PyTorch execution on Intel CPUs. By default, it uses Tensor Processing Primitives (TPP) (Georganas et al., 2021; Thangamani et al., 2025).

KTransformers (Chen et al., 2025): A framework for locally deployed MoE models with static CPU–GPU offloading: routed experts run on the CPU, while attention and shared experts run on the GPU. We use the SOSP’25 release.

vLLM (, 2026): A widely used LLM serving framework; we use its CPU-only variant (, 2026).

oneDNN (, 2025): Intel’s high-performance DNN primitive library; we use oneDNN 3.10.1.

7.3. Workloads

We evaluate HiNa-MoE at two levels: single-operator (FFN) kernels and end-to-end model inference.

FFN Kernel Evaluation. We extract the expert-matrix shapes from four MoE models: Mixtral-8x7B, Mixtral-8x22B (, 2025), DeepSeek-V3 (, 2025), and Qwen3-235B-A22B (, 2025). Their expert dimensions and routing configurations are summarized in Table 3. We report the geometric mean over 100 runs.

End-to-End Inference Evaluation. We measure end-to-end inference latency for Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen2-57B-A14B (Yang et al., 2024). We integrate HiNa-MoE by replacing the corresponding CPU operators in IPEX and KTransformers, yielding two configurations: HiNa-MoE (IPEX) and HiNa-MoE (KTrans). Unless otherwise stated, we use batch size 1 to reflect low-concurrency, latency-oriented deployments and to match prior work (Chen et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025). We report the geometric mean over 5 runs.

8. Evaluation Results

8.1. FFN Kernel Performance

We begin by evaluating the core MoE FFN operator under varying per-expert token counts, using the exact expert matrix shapes of real-world MoE models (Table 3).

Figure 10 shows that HiNa-MoE consistently outperforms all baselines. Averaged across all workloads, it achieves 1.73×\times and 1.68×\times speedups over IPEX and KTransformers, respectively, with maximum observed speedups of 3.37×\times and 2.16×\times. On the 6430, HiNa-MoE reaches up to 96% of the measured peak local memory bandwidth, suggesting that performance is close to the platform’s bandwidth ceiling. These gains come from (i) NUMA-aware task partitioning that avoids remote weight traffic and (ii) AMX micro-kernels that sustain high utilization while preserving general-purpose layouts. In contrast, oneDNN is slower due to the need to convert the weight matrices into an AMX-specific layout.

MoE FFN latency is largely insensitive to small changes in per-expert token count (e.g., 1∼\sim16 tokens). The dominant cost is streaming large expert weights from memory, whereas the gathered-token matrix 𝐈\mathbf{I} contributes little to the total traffic. KTransformers shows a slight throughput drop around 4 tokens, as it uses AMX only when an expert processes more than 4 tokens; otherwise, it falls back to AVX-512 (Chen et al., 2025). HiNa-MoE uses AMX efficiently even for single-token decoding.

HiNa-MoE’s advantage is more pronounced on the 6448H (4 sockets) than on the 6430 (2 sockets) because the 6448H has much lower cross-socket bandwidth (32 GB/s vs. 95 GB/s). Avoiding remote weight traffic therefore yields larger relative benefits as NUMA topologies become more complex.

We further evaluate the INT8-quantized FFN kernel. For a fair comparison, both HiNa-MoE and KTransformers use the same symmetric group-wise quantization scheme. As shown in Figure 11, HiNa-MoE achieves an average speedup of 2.18×\times over KTransformers, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach under INT8 precision as well.

8.2. End-to-end Inference Performance

Decoding Phase.We first evaluate end-to-end decoding performance for Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen2-57B-A14B with batch size 1, using 128 input and output tokens on a dual-socket 6430 CPU + RTX A6000 system. Figure 12 shows that HiNa-MoE achieves the highest decoding throughput, with average speedups of 1.99×\times, 1.70×\times, and 1.22×\times over vLLM (CPU-only), IPEX, and KTransformers, respectively, and maximum speedups of 2.87×\times, 2.09×\times, and 1.25×\times. For IPEX and KTransformers, we use their HiNa-MoE-integrated counterparts to isolate the impact of the CPU operator implementation. These gains are consistent with our FFN-kernel analysis: decoding is dominated by streaming expert weights from memory, making memory bandwidth and kernel efficiency critical. HiNa-MoE reduces cross-socket traffic through NUMA-aware task partitioning and improves kernel efficiency for small per-expert token counts compared with IPEX and KTransformers, respectively.

The results also highlight the benefit of preserving a general-purpose weight layout. Both oneDNN and HiNa-MoE keep expert weights in the general layout, but oneDNN performs weight-layout transformation at runtime for each inference, whereas HiNa-MoE fuses lightweight transformations into the existing token gather/store paths. Thus, HiNa-MoE avoids the recurring transformation overhead while retaining compatibility with standard CPU–GPU execution.

To examine whether these benefits persist beyond batch size 1, Figure 13 further reports decoding performance across different batch sizes. HiNa-MoE consistently outperforms IPEX over the evaluated range. This is expected because expert FFNs account for approximately 80% of the decoding runtime, making the optimized FFN execution the dominant contributor to end-to-end performance.

Prefill Phase.We next evaluate long-context prefill by integrating different CPU operator backends into SGLang (SGL) (Zheng et al., 2024) on the 6430 CPU + A6000 GPU system, using Qwen2-57B-A14B with batch size 1. During prefill, GQA attention runs on the GPU, while expert FFNs primarily run on the CPU. Table 4 reports the prefill throughput across input sequence lengths.

Without GPU scheduling, SGL+HiNa-MoE achieves performance comparable to SGL+KTransformers, showing that preserving the general-purpose weight layout does not sacrifice CPU-side execution efficiency. More importantly, this general layout also allows GPU scheduling without requiring expert-weight reconversion. We emphasize that we do not introduce a new scheduling policy; rather, HiNa-MoE’s layout compatibility enables SGLang to schedule expert execution on the GPU while retaining the same CPU backend. With GPU scheduling, SGL+HiNa-MoE consistently outperforms SGL+KTransformers across all evaluated sequence lengths, achieving speedups from 1.29×\times at 2K to 1.67×\times at 32K. These results demonstrate that HiNa-MoE provides both efficient CPU execution and the layout flexibility required for heterogeneous CPU–GPU inference.

Both SGL+HiNa-MoE and SGL+KTransformers exhibit a similar trend as the sequence length increases: their prefill throughput improves from 2K to 8K, peaks at 8K, and gradually decreases at 16K and 32K. This trend arises from the different scaling behaviors of GPU-side GQA attention and CPU-side expert FFN. As shown in Table 5, increasing the sequence length from 2K to 8K improves the effective computational performance of both operators, with attention increasing from 97.88 to 119.97 TFLOPS and FFN from 13.44 to 15.86 TFLOPS, indicating improved hardware utilization. Beyond 8K, however, the performance gains become marginal as both operators approach saturation. Meanwhile, GQA attention grows quadratically with the sequence length (O⁡(l2)O(l^{2})), whereas the expert FFN grows approximately linearly. As a result, the attention latency increases rapidly from 8.02 ms at 8K to 85.466 ms at 32K despite nearly saturated execution performance. Consequently, the rapidly increasing attention cost can no longer be offset by improved execution efficiency. Although FFN remains the dominant component, the growing attention overhead reduces the benefit of processing longer sequences, causing prefill throughput to decrease.

8.3. Ablation Study

We analyze the contribution of each component: the micro-kernel (+m), including FFN optimizations for both the general layout and page-interleaving, and the decode-phase attention optimization (+a). Figure 14 reports the decoding throughput improvement brought by each component at a batch size of 1, with IPEX serving as the baseline for Mixtral-8x7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, and KTransformers for Qwen2-57B-A14B.

Both optimizations improve performance, with micro-kernel optimization (+m) providing the largest gain and improving performance by 27% on average over the baseline. For Qwen2-57B-A14B, attention optimization provides no additional benefit because KTransformers offloads attention computation to the GPU, whereas (+a) targets the CPU-side attention path. In contrast, Qwen3-30B-A3B exhibits a more pronounced benefit from (+a), as its attention accounts for a larger fraction of the decoding computation than in Mixtral-8x7B, making CPU-side attention optimization more impactful on end-to-end performance. This result highlights that the effectiveness of attention optimization depends on both the relative cost of attention and the underlying offloading strategy.

8.4. Cross-NUMA Data Traffic Analysis

Using Linux perf, we quantify cross-socket traffic by measuring the fraction of L3-miss loads served by remote DRAM (mem_load_l3_miss_retired.remote_dram) among all DRAM-served L3-miss loads. Figure 15 shows that HiNa-MoE’s remote-access fraction is nearly zero, validating that our task partitioning (Section 5) largely eliminates remote accesses to weights. KTransformers also shows low remote traffic due to its manual weight partitioning. While oneDNN and IPEX exhibit similar remote fractions, oneDNN additionally pays runtime overhead for weight-layout transformations, leading to worse overall performance.

8.5. Evaluation on an HBM-based CPU

We evaluate FFN-kernel performance on a dual-socket Intel Xeon CPU Max 9462 (9462) (, 2025). Each socket provides 64 GB of HBM (HBM-only mode). The measured peak bandwidth is 853 GB/s; local NUMA accesses reach 425 GB/s, while cross-socket accesses drop to 89 GB/s.

Because HBM capacity is insufficient for full end-to-end MoE inference on our evaluated models, we report FFN-kernel results only. Figure 16 shows that HiNa-MoE outperforms oneDNN and IPEX by 9.65×\times and 3.41×\times on average. The larger gap on 9462 is explained by the higher penalty of remote accesses: the local-to-remote bandwidth ratio is ∼\sim5×\times on 9462 versus ∼\sim2.3×\times on 6430. As the cost of cross-socket accesses increases, HiNa-MoE’s NUMA-aware scheduling yields correspondingly larger benefits.

8.6. Integrating HiNa-MoE into MoE Inference Frameworks

Figure 17 summarizes the workflow of existing MoE inference frameworks. Integrating HiNa-MoE requires only two changes: (1) skip the weight pre-conversion step used by implementations based on the AMX-specific layout, and (2) replace the framework’s CPU-side attention and FFN operators with HiNa-MoE implementations. For example, in IPEX we replace the mixtral_moe_tpp_kernl_impl function responsible for FFN computation; in total, integration requires modifying about 30 lines of framework code.

9. Discussion and Future Work

Our evaluation shows that HiNa-MoE achieves consistent speedups across multi-socket servers and real-world MoE models. While the current implementation targets latency-oriented inference at small batch sizes on AMX-capable CPUs, the underlying design principles generalize.

Adaptation to other CPU architectures. HiNa-MoE’s core idea—preserve general-purpose weight layouts and adapt the computation kernels—extends beyond AMX. Prior work suggests that Arm’s SME can support tile-oriented micro-kernels similar in spirit to AMX (Deng et al., 2026). A natural direction is to apply the same “transform intermediate matrix 𝐈\mathbf{I}, not 𝐖\mathbf{W}” philosophy to SME by fusing lightweight layout transformations into token gathering and kernel execution, with tile sizes chosen to match the available register space and instruction semantics.

Multi-batch and CPU–GPU collaborative inference. For larger batch sizes and long-prompt prefill, CPU-only routed-expert execution can become a bottleneck because GPU compute and bandwidth are typically higher (Cao et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025). A promising direction is dynamic expert offloading based on prompt length, batch size, and available GPU memory, overlapping transfers with CPU computation (Yu et al., 2026). Because HiNa-MoE preserves general-purpose layouts and avoids framework-level allocator changes, experts can move between CPU and GPU without layout-conversion overhead, making it a natural substrate for such schedulers.

10. Conclusion

We have presented HiNa-MoE, a high-performance, non-intrusive operator library for MoE inference on multi-socket, multi-core CPUs. It preserves general-purpose matrix layouts for compatibility with CPU–GPU offloading frameworks, while improving performance through (1) AMX-efficient micro-kernels that fuse token gathering with lightweight, on-the-fly data movement, (2) NUMA-aware task partitioning that exploits the periodicity of interleaved pages without modifying the framework allocator, and (3) decode-phase attention optimization that converts memory-bound matrix–vector operations into compute-intensive matrix–matrix multiplications.

Across multiple server-class CPUs and real-world MoE models, HiNa-MoE achieves up to 3.37×\times FFN-kernel speedup and up to 2.09×\times end-to-end MoE inference speedup over state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining near-zero cross-socket traffic and plug-and-play integration.
